# Quality audit of the Dental Clinic AI Assistant

*Generated by `python -m qa.make_report` from the saved runs in `qa/results/`. Every number below is computed from those files. Full per-case records (all 8 fields you asked for): **[QA_CASES.md](QA_CASES.md)**.*

## Headline

* **265 test cases** in four rounds (every round has more than 30), covering all 10 categories you listed (plus unusual message styles).
* **First-run accuracy on messages the assistant had not been tuned on: 218/265 = 82.3%** (rounds 2-4 only, i.e. the fresh ones: 163/200 = 81.5%). **This is the number to believe.**
* **After the fixes: 264/265 = 99.6%** - but the assistant was repaired AGAINST these same cases, so this is the score on data it was tuned on. **It is not a prediction for real patients and it is not 100%.**
* **1 failure remains** (below). 32 defects were found and fixed (section 4). The 609 tests that existed before the audit still pass; the audit added 348 more (`tests/test_qa_suite.py`, `tests/test_qa_regressions.py`), 957 in total.
* In none of the 265 cases (first runs included) did the assistant send an unverified answer, a price or doctor that is not in the knowledge base, an internal marker, or a claim that an appointment was confirmed (an independent check runs on every case, separate from the validator). Those checks do not judge *relevance*: section 4 lists the irrelevant or wrong replies that were sent automatically and are now fixed.
* **One safety question needs your decision** (section 6): patients with an emergency get *no* automatic message, only a flagged item on the dashboard.

## 1. How the audit was run

1. **Expectations first.** For each case I wrote down what *should* happen (auto-reply / held for approval / escalated, which facts must appear, which must never appear, urgent or not) from the documented policy, *before* running it.
2. **Real pipeline.** Each message goes through `webhook.handle_incoming_message` (classify -> retrieve -> draft -> verify -> route), in a throw-away database and a throw-away copy of the knowledge base. Template mode (no Claude API key), simulated WhatsApp.
3. **Run, read, fix.** Baseline run; then I read **every answer by hand**, including the ones that passed (that found 6 more defects the expectations had missed); then fixed root causes, not the test strings.
4. **Fresh rounds to check the fixes generalise.** Rounds 2, 3 and 4 were written *after* the previous round's fixes and *not run until finished*. The first run of each is the honest measurement; the same cases were then used to drive more fixes.
5. **Independent safety invariants** on every case regardless of its own expectation: an auto-reply has no failed check and equals the verified draft; a held message only ever got a fixed notice; every ₹ amount sent exists in the knowledge base; every doctor named exists; no internal markers (`SOURCES:`, `treatment:`...); no claim that an appointment is confirmed/booked/available.
6. **Mutation check.** I reverted 8 of the fixes one at a time and confirmed the new tests fail each time (one fix was initially not covered; I added a test and re-checked).

Notes on the table:
* Round 1's baseline used my *original* expectations. 12 of its 65 cases fail when scored with the final, stricter expectations (reading the answers by hand exposed flaws the original expectations were too lenient to notice): **53/65 = 81.5%**.
* The first-run score did **not** improve from round to round (84.6% -> 81.3% -> 79.5% -> 84.6%). Each fresh set exposed new gaps (mostly vocabulary: Hinglish words, phrasings). That is the signature of a keyword-and-pattern system: fixes are real, but the next real patient will find the next gap. My cases are deliberately hard and adversarial, so real traffic may do better on plain questions and worse on messy ones; this data cannot say which. Treat ~80% as the honest working figure until the vocabulary is built from real messages.
* Test/harness errors are my mistakes (a test that searched for the word 'confirmed' inside the clinic's own policy sentence; an audit-runner bug). They are *included* in the measured figure and listed in section 5.

### What the first-run failures were (all rounds)

| Kind of failure | Count |
|---|---:|
| sent automatically but should have been held | 9 |
| wrong or incomplete answer sent automatically | 4 |
| emergency not flagged urgent | 7 |
| over-cautious: held something that could be answered | 17 |
| wrong label or poor draft (held for a person) | 2 |
| test or harness error (not the assistant's fault) | 8 |

The first two rows are the ones that matter: a message that reached a patient and should not have, or was wrong. Over-cautious failures cost reception time but never harm a patient.

## 3. Failures that remain

**R-G2: 'Since the clinic is open all day on Sundays, I will come at 5 PM'**  
The clinic closes at 2 PM on Sundays. On its FIRST run this case passed (the assistant auto-replied with the true opening hours, which corrects the patient's mistake). After fix F16 ('I will come' is a booking request) the message is held for a person instead, and the draft shows the real hours but also echoes the requested time ('around Sunday 5 pm'). My expectation says the draft must not echo it, so the case now fails. The assistant does not compare a requested time with the opening hours, because the hours are stored as free text.  
*Impact:* Low: a person always reviews it, nothing is sent or confirmed. It is a case where a later fix made one behaviour slightly worse.

Cases failing in the final run: `R-G2`. It is recorded as a strict *expected failure* in `tests/test_qa_suite.py` (if it is ever fixed the test will say so, and the entry must be removed).

Weaknesses that are **not** failures of any test case, but which the audit saw and did not fix (section 6 has the decisions I need from you):

* **Emergency patients get no automatic message.** An emergency is escalated and flagged urgent, but nothing is sent until a person approves. If nobody is watching the dashboard, the patient hears nothing. (Decision needed, below.)
* **Devanagari (Hindi/Marathi script) is never answered automatically** - it goes to a person (it is handled safely, not understood).
* **Vocabulary is finite.** Every fresh round found new Hinglish/Marathi words, phrasings and typos the rules did not know (several per round). Marathi in particular has had almost no coverage beyond a few words.
* **Typo repair covers about 60 topic keywords,** one letter off. Other misspellings fall back to 'I don't have that information' (safe, but reception handles them).
* **'refund' is treated as a complaint,** so 'What is your refund policy?' gets a held draft that apologises for the patient's 'experience'. A person sees it, nothing is sent.
* **A doctor's weekly timetable is not their presence on a given day.** Date-specific questions are now held, but a question like 'Is Dr. Rahul there on Saturdays?' is answered with the timetable (which is a fact in the knowledge base).
* **Booking drafts echo the day the patient wrote** ('around Kal', 'around Monday wednesday'); cosmetic, held for a person anyway.
* **Replies are long when several topics are asked** (up to about 1,600 characters); fine for WhatsApp, not elegant.

## 5. Every change to an expectation (so you can check the tests were not bent to fit)

| Cases | Kind | Was | Now | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D5, E1, E2, E3, E4, E6 | test error | must_not_contain 'confirmed' | must_not_match a regex for CLAIMS of confirmation ("is confirmed", "I've booked"...), with an exception for the clinic's own policy sentence | The clinic's real policy text says "Appointments are confirmed by our reception team". A plain substring test flagged that true sentence. The assistant was behaving correctly in all six; the test was too blunt. |
| A5 | tightened | only checked the crown price was present | also: the reply must not contain the Root Canal and Implant price blocks | The reply listed three treatments' prices for a question about one (found by reading it). |
| E1 | tightened | no duplicate check | "Dr. Neha Joshi –" at most once | The same doctor card appeared twice in the draft. |
| F3 | tightened | no intent check | intent must be 'unknown' | An off-topic question was labelled treatment_info (routing was right, the label was wrong). |
| G2, J1 | tightened | reply must not say 'free' | reply must also state the real price | The reply described the treatment but never corrected the patient's claim that it is free. |
| G5 | tightened | any route allowed | must be held for a person | The patient quotes a promise from staff and asks the clinic to honour it; auto-answering with the list price ignored that. |
| G7, J6 | tightened | any route allowed | must be held (G7 also: must say the doctor was not found) | The patient names a doctor who does not exist; a person should see that. |
| S-H1 | test error | must not match `you can` | must not match `you can (get/have/go ahead/safely)`, `it is safe` | The assistant's standard medical reply says 'You can also call us on...'; the pattern was too blunt (found in round 3). |
| S-D6 | harness bug | - | runner only reads replies to the current message | The runner picked up the reply to the earlier message of the same patient. |

No expectation was ever loosened to make an assistant failure pass. The 'tightened' rows made the tests *stricter*; the 'test error' rows corrected tests that were wrong about what the clinic's own text says.

## 6. Limits of this audit, and decisions I need from you

* **Template mode only.** All cases ran with `USE_LLM = False`. The Claude-written-answer path (and its SOURCES/ANSWER protocol) was **not** exercised; no API key was available. Before enabling it, run these cases again with a key and `APPROVE_MODEL_ANSWERS=true`.
* **I wrote the system and the tests.** Same author, same blind spots. The fresh rounds reduce, but cannot remove, that bias. Real, anonymised patient messages from reception are the right next test set.
* **The 'after fixes' figure is not an accuracy estimate.** The fixes were made against those cases. The first-run figures on fresh cases are.
* **Meta WhatsApp Cloud API was not part of this audit** (it is still untested against real Meta servers; see `WHATSAPP_CLOUD_SETUP.md`). Message formats WhatsApp adds (voice, images, location, reactions) are handled by separate code covered by earlier tests, not by these cases.
* **Dummy clinic data.** Prices, doctors and hours are the sample data; the audit checks the machinery, not the clinic's real facts.
* **DECISION 1 - emergency acknowledgement.** Should an emergency message get an automatic fixed reply right away (for example: 'If you have heavy bleeding, trouble breathing or swallowing, or a facial injury, go to the nearest hospital emergency department now. Our team has been alerted and will reply as soon as possible. You can also call +91...'), while still flagging it urgent for a person? It is safer for the patient than silence, but it is a medical-safety statement the *clinic* should approve. I did not add it without your decision.
* **DECISION 2 - start in shadow mode.** Given ~80-85% first-run accuracy, I recommend running with auto-reply OFF (every reply approved by a person) for a few weeks on real messages, measuring with this same harness, and only then enabling auto-reply for the safest topics (hours, location, prices, doctors).

## 7. How to repeat it

```bash
./.venv/bin/python -m qa.run_qa --round all            # run every case, print failures
./.venv/bin/python -m qa.run_qa --only A1 R-D5 --verbose    # look at single cases
./.venv/bin/python -m qa.run_qa --round all --json qa/results/all_final.json && ./.venv/bin/python -m qa.make_report
./.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q                              # all tests, including the audit cases
```

To add a case: copy a `Case(...)` line in `qa/cases*.py`, write the expectation **before** running it, and run. Real messages from your reception team are worth far more than anything I can invent: add them here.
